# Re-merging the SAME branch: merge theirs into ours, theirs then adds another
# commit, merge theirs again. The first merge re-signs theirs' rebased entries,
# so the second merge must still locate the shared base against ours (it no longer
# matches by signature). Both of theirs' changes must survive and the twice-merged
# log must verify.

exec git init
exec git config user.email test@sesam.dev
exec git config user.name 'Sesam Test'

exec sesam init --user admin --install-merge
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'init sesam'

exec sesam tell --user bob --recipient $BOB_PUBKEY --group dev
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'base: bob'

# OURS diverges with its own user.
exec git checkout -b ours
exec sesam tell --user carol --recipient $CAROL_PUBKEY --group dev
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'ours: carol'

# THEIRS: first change.
exec git checkout -b theirs ours~1
exec sesam user change-groups --user bob --group-add ops
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'theirs: bob += ops'

# Merge #1, finalized. sesam.yml takes ours via the sesam-ours merge driver
# (config-regen from the merged log is a separate, tracked follow-up), so there
# is nothing to resolve by hand: git stops via pre-merge-commit, `git commit`
# finalizes.
exec git checkout ours
! exec git merge theirs
exec git commit --no-edit
exec sesam verify

# THEIRS gets a SECOND change on top of the already-merged branch.
exec git checkout theirs
exec sesam user change-groups --user bob --group-add sec
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'theirs: bob += sec'

# Merge #2 - the re-merge that used to fail with "failed to find common origin".
exec git checkout ours
! exec git merge theirs
exec git commit --no-edit

# Both of theirs' changes are in the twice-merged log, which verifies end to end.
exec sesam verify
exec sesam show .sesam/audit/log.jsonl
stdout 'ops'
stdout 'sec'
